# The PsycheAI read: what it contains and the standards it meets

The format of the PsycheAI read the user asked for: a personality read from their own Instagram, which they connected and chose to share. It describes the document and the standards a good one meets, written with the assistant's own judgement and returned to publish_psyche as one JSON object matching the schema.

## Sources
- The user's own Instagram: posts, captions, stories and highlights, bio, the comments they wrote, and, only if they allowed it, their message threads.
- Their own Facebook, and their Messenger threads, only when they added them (below).
- What others wrote is only context for their replies: never quoted, described or judged, and no other person is named: "a close friend", "a sibling".
- The user is written as `PsycheUser` wherever their name or handle would go; their real name is put back on their device.
- **Text only.** The read is written from words and dates: captions, comments, messages, the bio, any text added on top of a story or post (typed, pasted or in a text sticker, read in full), and when things were posted. The photos and videos themselves are not analysed: nothing is read from faces, bodies, looks, clothes, surroundings or who appears in them. A story with no words on it counts only for its date.

## Reading plan
A read is only as good as its sample, and the first items a feed returns are the newest, not the most telling, so a read is spread across the whole span. The sample is the digest the skill keeps (`digest/digest.md`): each line is one dated thing they wrote, with its time when Instagram gives one, and the read is written from it, so everything the read cites is a line in it. The digest grows over reads towards about 200,000 characters of the person's own words at most. A read takes about 7 to 10 minutes: it reads to its target in the largest pages the tools give and writes the digest as it goes.
- **A first read aims for about 110,000 characters:** posts and stories about 35,000 (their comments included), their own messages about 50,000 and what they answer about 25,000, when they agreed. **Each later read adds about 40,000**, oldest first where the digest is thinnest, until the shares below are reached. A target is what a read reaches, not a ceiling to stop short of; only an account with less to read stops sooner.
- **Posts and stories, up to about 85,000 characters in all:** a caption or comment under about 30 characters (an emoji, "Sunday vibes", "nice one") counts for its date, not as words, as on psycheai.io; then every longer caption of their own (a very long one up to its first 1,500 characters); the text on stories and highlights across every year the account has, not just the latest pages (no single year more than about a quarter of the sample when there are four or more years; keep going back until the oldest year is reached) (a story with no words isn't opened: its date comes with the list); and up to about 15,000 characters of comments they wrote. Past the ceiling, the sample is thinned evenly across the years, not cut at the oldest.
- **Messages, only when the person agreed, up to about 115,000 characters of their own in all:** the 10 busiest conversations in their inbox, judged by how much is in each, not by which is newest: measure them, since the inbox lists newest first. A conversation comes newest first and can't skip to a year, so depth goes where it counts: the 4 busiest are paged back as far as their target reaches (about 9,000 characters each on a first read, growing over later reads to about 15,000, until their first year is reached); the other 6 are read from their recent pages (about 2,300 each, growing to about 6,000). When those 10 hold less than the messages target (some are short, or end early), the next busiest are read too until it is reached: "(whole thread)" covers one conversation, never the total. From each page, keep the most telling of their own messages (composed ones, plans, feelings, apologies, questions; never "ok" or "haha"), each with what it answers before it as "> " lines, names as "Friend". A message sent word for word to several people (an announcement, a request to follow an account) is one thing they did, kept once. Long pasted or forwarded text (over about 800 characters) and messages that are mostly a link are not their own words and are left out. Which conversations, and how many were read, is never evidence about them.
- **The bio and the counts** (posts, stories, comments, conversations, and Instagram's own totals for followers, following and saved when it shows them): about 5,000 characters.
- Room the messages leave unused, or all of it when messages weren't shared, goes to posts and stories, never the other way.
- **Likes, saves, follows and searches:** a light look, for interests only and not counted as their words: the accounts they like and save most, the hashtags they meet most, Instagram's topics for them and their most repeated searches, about 15,000 characters at most.

## Facebook they added
Only when the user added it (Facebook, and their Messenger threads if they chose it), through Muse's own Facebook connection, read like their Instagram and kept in the same digest: their own posts as "[facebook post]" lines among the posts and stories, their comments among the comments, and Messenger conversations, headed "Messenger", ranked with Instagram's by how much is in each, within the same shares. A habit seen on both is one pattern seen twice.

## WhatsApp chats they added
Only when the user added them, and only as the file the skill made ready on their own device (`sources/whatsapp.txt`, from `bin/psyche.py prep`), never the export itself:
- It holds their own messages, each dated, after what they answer as "> " lines (context only); everyone else is "Friend A", "Friend B" and so on, and numbers, emails, links and handles are already taken out.
- Up to three chats, about 45,000 characters each for one or two, 30,000 each for three (75,000 each in a Deep Psyche), counted as conversations of their own in the messages share, which grows by the same amount.
- Where WhatsApp and Instagram show the same habit, it is one pattern seen twice, and stronger for it, not two.
- The read never names a friend or writes "Friend A": "a long-running chat with a close friend", "a group chat of six". The confidence rationale counts the chats with the rest ("and three WhatsApp chats, 2018 to 2026").

## Evidence, strongest first
When two signals disagree, the stronger one wins and the read says so ("follows a dozen running accounts but no run since 2021").
1. Sustained, repeated action across years: a subject they keep returning to, a habit that recurs, a person they keep writing to.
2. Their own composed words: captions, comments, their own messages, the bio. The richest evidence there is.
3. Rhythm: when and how often they post (the times on the digest's lines), whether they publish or mostly watch.
4. Repeated engagement with others' work: accounts and topics they keep returning to.
5. A single like, follow or save: close to worthless alone.
6. Platform-guessed topics: weakest of all.

Two rules hold throughout:
- **One instance is not a pattern, and the count belongs in the sentence.** "Forty-odd captions across four years", "two mentions, both in 2019": a reader can weigh a claim with a number and cannot weigh "several".
- **Absence is not evidence.** Someone who never posts about family may be private. A blank is read as a finding only where that part of life would be expected to show.

## Who a sentence is about
The author of a caption is not automatically its subject. A story about a friend's new job, car or achievement is evidence about the friend; about the user it shows who they are around, what they notice and admire, and how they write about people. An account largely about other people is itself a finding: the connector, the observer, the one holding the camera. A comment on someone else's post is about that person.

## Time
- Each interest and value has a trajectory from the dates: structural (across the whole span and recently), stable, rising, declining, dormant (nothing for about two years: said plainly, not flattered) or phasic (ran for a window and stopped).
- Reduced posting is not a reduced life: where it matters, the read says the posts stopped, not that the interest did.

## Character
The character (`essence.character`) is matched on temperament, drive and how they treat people, never on looks. Not every character is open to everyone. First judge, privately, whether this person is most likely a woman or a man, from how they present themselves in their own data and their Meta account details — their name, pronouns in a bio, how they write about themselves, how friends address them. A woman gets one of: Mulan, Elsa, Moana, Rapunzel, Judy Hopps, Joy, Wonder Woman, Princess Peach, Hermione Granger, Sailor Moon, Hello Kitty, Kuromi. A man gets one of: Simba, Nick Wilde, Dr Watson, Buzz Lightyear, Odysseus, Captain America, Spider-Man, Hulk, Sherlock Holmes, Shrek, Po, Hiccup. Either may also get one of the characters who are neither: Baymax, The Tin Man, Remy, Pikachu. If you cannot tell with reasonable confidence, or they present as neither, choose only from those four. Then find the closest temperament among the ones open to them. This judgement chooses the character and nothing else: never state, hint at or explain it anywhere you write — not on the card, not in why they are like the character, not in any section or piece of evidence. Name the character by name alone, never with the studio, company or franchise behind them (Marvel, Disney, Pixar and the like), in anything you write.

## Type and traits
- Each MBTI letter is held only as strongly as its evidence: a lean is written as a lean.
- Each ledger row's `row` is an id from the guide's `rubric`, for that axis, exactly as spelled there; a row with any other id is dropped when the letters are scored.
- E/I is scored on the rubric's rows: their own words about their energy and the settings they choose weigh most, and initiating gatherings, even for the same friends, is a very slight lean to E. Never E/I evidence: message volume or length, when they are active, how many conversations were read (the reading plan chooses that number), whether the account is private, or that their circle is close (loyalty, not energy). How many people they keep up with counts when it is measured against everyone they message ("about 10 of your 140 threads run for years"). When the real signals point both ways, the letter is a slight lean, said so.
- S/N, T/F and J/P each rest on behaviour that bears on that axis alone; one fact is used for one letter.
- Big Five scores run 0 to 100, 50 being average, and agree with the letters they track (extraversion with E/I, openness with S/N, agreeableness with T/F, conscientiousness with J/P). "Neuroticism" is written as "emotional sensitivity", never as a defect.

## Writing
- Second person ("you"), warm and specific, honest about uncertainty, never sycophantic or moralising; things they may not know about themselves, including the unflattering but fair.
- Specific beats general: "your posting spikes on Saturday mornings and half your captions mention a trail" is worth reading; "you love the outdoors" is not.
- Plain words and short sentences. British spelling. Sentence case for every name and title ("The quiet organiser"). No filler words: profound, remarkable, journey, tapestry, navigate, leverage, truly.
- Each piece of evidence is used once in a section and at most twice in the whole read; one fact, one figure everywhere.

## Depth
What separates a read worth keeping from a summary of someone's feed:
- **Moments, not tallies.** Each section rests on specific things they did or wrote, each a line in the digest, in a phrase with its date ("the March 2024 caption on finishing a first half-marathon in the rain"), paraphrased, never anyone else's words. An evidence item is one such moment ("your May 2025 comment fixing a friend's recipe, gram by gram"), never the reading itself ("10 sampled conversations", "across 140 conversations", "the digest shows") or a summary of many ("long chats about work and travel"). If an item would still be true with the date taken out, it is a summary: use the one moment that shows it best. A count backs a moment up; it is not insight on its own. Message length and per-topic counts say little about a person: use each at most once in the whole read.
- **Say what it means.** Every finding answers "so what": what it suggests they want, protect, avoid or are working out, and how that shows up in their life. Name the tension between two things that are both true of them; that is usually where the insight is.
- **Written to them, about them.** Every line speaks to the person as "you", evidence items and ledger rows included ("you start most conversations in your top threads"): never he, she, they, "the user" or their name, and never a guess at their gender. About the person, not the dataset: Not "in the record", "in the sampled messages" or "the data shows". What was not read is said once, in the confidence rationale, never in each section.
- **Across the years.** Where the sample spans several years, each pattern, letter and section draws its evidence from more than one of them, the earlier years included, not only the latest; a theme seen in 2019 and again in 2026 is stronger than one seen twice in 2026, and the read says so. Each pattern's evidence items carry at least two different years, one of them before the latest two, whenever the digest spans three years or more; a theme found in one year is a phase, never a pattern.
- **Names only they fit.** A pattern's name says what this person does, in their own terms ("Fixes it before anyone asks", "Says yes, then works out how"); one that would fit thousands of people ("The curious connector") is renamed. Interests and values each name something particular to them ("Restoring old film cameras", "Rest is earned, not owed"); two that overlap ("Friends and shared meals" beside "Food and dining") are one.
- **Commit where the evidence does.** A score sits where the evidence puts it; it is not pulled towards 50 to be safe. A trait with no evidence goes near 50 with low confidence, and the rationale says so. The test for every paragraph: a close friend would recognise them in it and still learn something; one that would fit anyone with the same interests is rewritten.

## Wellness
A read of behaviour across six dimensions, never a health assessment.
- **lifeTrajectory:** the phase and the arc across the whole span, not the last months. Name a hard stretch plainly (when it started, how long, what changed, whether they came through); never invent its cause, and a gap in posting is ambiguous (a new baby or job as often as grief).
- **outlook:** from their own words, not reposts: plans as expectation or hope, setbacks as temporary or permanent. Use the real word when it fits (bleak, grim, worn down); a feed is partly performance, and deadpan humour is a style, not despair.
- **socialConnection:** distinct people, reach beyond a set circle, and whether it runs both ways; giving far more than they get back is named gently.
- **cognitiveLoad:** how many threads and plans they carry and whether plans close out; apparent load, never capacity.
- **meaning:** what they return to over years and whether stated commitments match behaviour.
- **rhythmAndActivity:** posting times are when they reached for a phone, never a sleep record; activity only from what they chose to post, and silence is not a finding.
Bands describe a pattern, not a person; most people are `mixed` on most. `under strain` needs a pattern the evidence shows; `not enough evidence` is a real answer. `overall` is prose: no score, index, grade or average. `suggestions` are what an observant friend would suggest this week, never treatment. No condition is named, implied or predicted; where something looks like it warrants one, say it is worth taking to someone who can assess it.

## Attachment
A leaning (secure, anxious or avoidant, or two of them, as "anxious-leaning, with avoidant edges"), never fearful-avoidant or disorganised, shown working.
- From conduct with people: who starts conversations, how fast and warmly they reply, how they write to those closest, what happens around a gap, how large a circle and for how long. What they watch or save about relationships is an interest, one supporting line at most.
- About half of adults lean secure, so a non-secure leaning must show in their own conduct, and a mixed one needs both halves visible. When thin or mixed, take the cautious read ("leans secure, with avoidant defences under stress"), and name in `why` the stronger style considered and what would have moved the read to it.
- Lead with what the style is good at, then its costs as tendencies they can work with: what it looks like, what helps, and that it moves. It is the most changeable thing in the read.

## Ideal partner
Argued from the attachment read above, not a fresh read. `needs`: three to five requirements that follow from their attachment, love languages and relationship strengths and weaknesses, each with its evidence, not pleasant adjectives. `carefulOf`: two to four partner types or dynamics that would predictably go wrong for this person, and what that would look like, not universal red flags. The test: if a line would fit a stranger with a different attachment style, it has not used the read. `summary`: the honest verdict in two or three sentences, not a recap. No private person is named; describe the relationship ("the friend they write to most").

## Career
A coach deciding what they should do next, a different job from the how-they-work section: a sentence that would sit there belongs there.
- `situation`: where they appear to be, from the work they mention, the rooms they are in and what they are building. Where their own words show their field (its jargon, a workplace joke, the deadlines they mention, a deal or a launch talked through with a colleague), it names that field first, in plain words a stranger would use ("accounting", "nursing"), never traits ("analytical, high-stakes work"), messages and added chats counting as much as captions; the edge, fit and actions start from it, and the first kind of work under `fit.suits` is in or beside that field. There is no CV, title, employer or salary here: infer openly and say so, and where work barely shows, say that and keep the section short.
- `edge`: the centre. What they do reliably that most people do not, as an advantage they can use, with real counts ("the same twelve people close for four years"). One that would fit any organised, kind or hard-working person is a compliment, not an edge.
- `underused`: what they have and visibly don't use. `holdingBack`: the pattern most likely to cost them at work, from behaviour, not a label; direct about the pattern, never the person.
- `fit`: kinds of work that suit and that would drain, each with its reason from their data; never one job title, nothing about pay or status, and draining is a mismatch, not a fault.
- Who-is-this-about bites hardest here: photographing founders at a demo night makes them the person in the room, not a founder.

## Development and the plan
- `development` closes the read by resolving the patterns: `buildOn`, two strengths to lean into; `develop`, two areas worth working on. Each names the pattern it resolves and `raisedBy`, the sections that raised it.
- A `develop` area is often a strength that turns costly under pressure (independence that becomes going it alone). It carries `earlySigns`, two behaviours someone could notice early, not feelings; `counterMove`, one concrete move for that moment; and `reflect`, one open question specific to them. Behaviour under pressure, never a condition.
- **One plan of about five actions:** the develop actions, `careerAssessment.actions` and `wellness.suggestions` together, one or two from each. Every horizon has at least one: this week, this quarter, this year. Each is a first move, not an ambition ("ask your manager which of the three projects counts at review", not "increase your visibility"). No two are the same step, including the same step on a different deadline.
- Nothing in development or the plan makes a claim no section made.

## Thin evidence
Posts and stories alone, mostly pictures with few words, support rhythm and the people around them far better than inner life, work or relationships. Where a section's evidence is thin, it says so in a sentence and stays short; it is never padded with general statements that could describe anyone. A short, true section is better than a long, generic one.

## Limits
- Insight and coaching only: never therapy, treatment or a diagnosis, and no clinical terms. The wellness section is a read of behaviour (posting times, activity, connection), not a health assessment.
- Not inferred unless the user stated it in their own words: sexual orientation, health, immigration status, political affiliation, religion. Nobody is classified by appearance or by who they follow.
- Anything printed on the card (headline, card lines, pattern names) is positive or neutral, and never about romance or dating.
- The send-up (`bonus`) is deliberately blunt: pointed and funny, about habits and the gaps between plans and follow-through, with no softening; its `advice` is where the kindness goes. It is never about health, appearance, identity or anyone else, and if the user seems to be going through a hard time it sticks to small, harmless habits.

## Confidence
Start from the sources (the digest header's `sources`, and WhatsApp chats if added), never lowering it for how much was read. Instagram, its messages included: 65 to 79. With Facebook or WhatsApp chats, 72 to 86; with both, 76 to 90; never above 90. Within it, higher when they write in their own words across years and the sources agree; lower when it is mostly stories and pictures or a short span. Below it only for a thin account. `level`: high from 75, moderate 60 to 74, low 40 to 59. The rationale names what was read and what was not, and `basedOn` lists it in the digest header's counts: "posts and stories" together (never which they are), conversations and their own messages, comments, the interests and Instagram's totals when the digest has them, and rhythm only as from the lines read, never complete ("239 posts and stories, 141 with words").

## Before saving
A last pass over the whole read; most weak reads fail one of these:
- **Range.** A theme that explains a lot is a pattern; the other sections show other sides of them, not the same theme again. No one theme anchors more than three sections, counting the patterns, how they work, what holds them back, development, the plan and the send-up.
- **No repeats.** No two items in one list say the same thing (two "what holds you back" entries about spreading thin are one), and no two actions are the same task. A field with nothing new to say stays short; it never restates another.
- **Every citation is in the digest.** Each dated moment the read cites is a line in `digest/digest.md`. One that isn't comes out, or goes into the digest first from their Instagram.
- **One count everywhere.** Every count in the read is the digest header's, and `basedOn` misses no source the digest holds.
- **Their field, by name.** Where the digest shows what they work in, `careerAssessment.situation` names it plainly and `fit.suits` starts beside it.
- **Every evidence item is a dated moment of theirs,** never a count of conversations or a mention of the digest or the sample.
- **Each pattern spans the years:** two different years, one before the latest two, once the digest spans three.

## Output
One JSON object that matches the schema, and nothing around it.
read.rubric:
**E/I**

| row | evidence | points to | weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| `own-words` | Their own words about their energy: introvert or extravert; crowds drain them, or they come alive in one. Calling themselves mixed, both or an ambivert: enter it under both letters, and the axis stays slight. | E or I | strong |
| `setting` | The setting they choose: strangers and big events — parties, mixers, conferences, meeting new people (E) / small familiar groups, avoiding mixers and strangers, tiring in unfamiliar settings (I). Seeing several groups of friends they already have is not this row. | E or I | strong |
| `reach-out` | Starts plans and conversations with people beyond their usual circle (E) / declines invitations, leaves early (I). Plans for the same friends are `convenes-known-circle`. | E or I | medium |
| `pursuits` | Chooses group pursuits (E) / chooses solitary pursuits over group ones (I). A sport or hobby with friends is common to everyone. | E or I | weak |
| `many-people` | Many distinct people engaged with (comments, the most-engaged list). | E | weak |
| `initiates` | Who starts the conversations, across their chats: they open most of them (E) / the other side usually does (I). Once for all their chats, not per chat. | E or I | weak |
| `convenes-known-circle` | Initiating gatherings — dinners, sport, trips — for a familiar circle: a very slight lean to E, once however often. | E | weak |

**N/S**

| row | evidence | points to | weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| `own-words` | Their own words about how they think: a big-picture person (N) / a details, facts person (S). | N or S | strong |
| `theorises` | Their own writing speculates, theorises, links unrelated fields, asks what something means. | N | medium |
| `captions-meaning` | Captions that go past the record to meaning, analogy or pattern — a clear share of them. | N | medium |
| `compares-tracks` | Compares specs and options before deciding; tracks exact figures, keeps records — outside their job: the numbers their work runs on are a topic, not a thinking style. | S | weak |
| `practical-craft` | Practical skills built step by step and kept up; sensory craft (food, tools, materials) for its own sake. A sport's technique does not count: every sport has one. | S | weak |
| `watches` | Watches long explanation — essays, analysis (N) / how-to, repair, recipes (S). | N or S | weak |
| `shared-words` | Words they choose to pass on — quotes, book passages, titles they name or search for: symbol, meaning, what lies under the surface, a fable like The Little Prince (N) / practical, factual, step by step (S). Once for all of it; their own writing outranks it. | N or S | weak |
| `abstract-topics` | Instagram's topics spread across many unrelated abstract subjects. | N | weak |

**T/F**

| row | evidence | points to | weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| `own-words` | Their own words about how they decide: logic (T) / how people feel (F). | T or F | strong |
| `tie-break` | A decision where the tie-break shows: a criterion, price or spec (T) / the effect on a person, a loyalty (F). | T or F | strong |
| `public-verdict` | A criticism, ranking or verdict made in public anyway, where the platform discourages it. | T | medium |
| `private-softening` | In private, holding back a criticism to protect a relationship; smoothing conflict. | F | medium |
| `credit` | Crediting others for what they achieved (T) / for what they are like (F). | T or F | weak |
| `captions-to-nobody` | Captions written to nobody in particular: verdicts (T) / feeling and who was there (F). | T or F | weak |
| `attention` | Attention mostly on subjects (T) / mostly on people (F). | T or F | weak |
| `shared-words` | Words they choose to pass on — quotes, book passages, titles: argument, systems, how things work (T) / feeling, worth, how people are treated (F). Once for all of it; their own writing outranks it. | T or F | weak |

**J/P**

| row | evidence | points to | weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| `own-words` | Their own words about planning: "I need a plan", "lock it in" (J) / "let's see", "I hate fixed plans" (P). | J or P | strong |
| `plans-ahead` | Bookings and itineraries made well ahead; deadlines named and met; lists, trackers, spreadsheets. | J | medium |
| `last-minute` | Same-day plans, short-notice trips; cancellable bookings chosen to keep options open; changing course. | P | medium |
| `decisions` | Decisions closed quickly and kept (J) / left open (P). | J or P | medium |
| `parallel-projects` | Several projects started in parallel and left open. | P | weak |
| `search-horizon` | Searches that plan ahead, "flights in March" (J) / for now, "open now", "tonight" (P). | J or P | weak |
| `saved-returned` | Saved posts returned to. | J | weak |

score.description: 0-100, for how well the data the reader gave supports this profile, starting from the sources they loaded — not lowered for how much of it was sampled.

rationale.description: One or two sentences on what the data does and does not support. Never cite a raw total as evidence of coverage: how many messages exist is a fact about the account, how many you read is a fact about your evidence.

basedOn.description: Two to four short phrases naming the sources this score rests on, each stating what you saw of what exists, read off coverage.sampling — "436 of 442 captions", "300 of 9,741 own messages", "complete hour-of-day and month-by-month histograms".

axis.description: One of: E/I, N/S, T/F, J/P.

row.description: The id of the rubric row this evidence fits, exactly as the rubric for this axis spells it.

pointsTo.description: The letter this piece points to (one of this axis's two letters), or "neutral" for a row that counts neither way.

note.description: The evidence itself, in a short clause under about 15 words, with its count or their quoted words; with neither it counts as weak.

ledger.description: Every piece of evidence you found for EITHER letter on this axis, each tagged with its rubric row — the ones against the letter you expect as carefully as the ones for it.

why.description: Two or three sentences, one paragraph, written together with the `evidence` list that follows and printed above it, never repeating it.

evidence.description: Three or four of the ledger's strongest pieces for this letter, printed as a list under the paragraph.

choice.description: The letter you conclude, weighing the ledger (the rubric's weights are a guide; you decide). The `why` above must argue this same letter.

strength.description: How far the weighed evidence leans: `clear` where the other side has little to offer, `moderate` where this side is clearly ahead on several solid pieces, otherwise `slight`; `slight` when their own words put them on both sides.

type.description: The type the four letters above spell, or Uncertain. One of: "INTJ", "INTP", "ENTJ", "ENTP", "INFJ", "INFP", "ENFJ", "ENFP", "ISTJ", "ISFJ", "ESTJ", "ESFJ", "ISTP", "ISFP", "ESTP", "ESFP", "Uncertain".

nickname.description: The common name for this type, e.g. "The Advocate". Empty string if the type is Uncertain.

caveat.description: One or two sentences on how much weight to put on this, including that MBTI is popular rather than validated.

reading.description: One sentence: the specific behaviour from the data that sets this score, as it shows in their week. No list of evidence: the score and this line are all the report prints.

id.description: p1, p2, p3 in order of how much of the report each explains. One of: "p1", "p2", "p3".

name.description: A short, memorable name in plain words, e.g. "The quiet organiser" or "Warm in small circles". It is printed on the card they share, so neutral or positive: the behaviour, never a fault.

line.description: One sentence saying what the pattern is: the behaviour, and the two sides of it — where it helps them and where it costs them. Nothing about romance or dating.

evidence.description: Two to four specific things from the digest that show it, each with a count or a proportion. Follow the rules on numbers: never a count of conversations they ever wrote in as breadth.

showsUpIn.description: The sections where this pattern visibly operates — at least three, or it is a finding rather than a pattern.

trajectory.description: How this has moved across the span of the data.

lastSeen.description: The year of the most recent evidence for this, as four digits, e.g. "2024". Empty string only when literally nothing cited carries a date.

detail.description: One sentence on how this shows up for them, with a count or a span in it; a trajectory other than structural or stable said in words.

interests.description: Strongest first. The report prints every one, a line each, under what drives them.

beliefs.description: Exactly one when values has two, to make up the third entry: religious, political, ethical or philosophical, as the data supports, and not covered by any value, motivator or pattern.

trajectory.description: How this has moved across the span of the data.

lastSeen.description: The year of the most recent evidence for this, as four digits, e.g. "2024". Empty string only when literally nothing cited carries a date.

detail.description: One or two sentences on what this looks like in practice for them.

evidence.description: What in the data supports it, with the count and the span in it.

values.description: Two distinct values, strongest first, and a third only when no belief is supported — exactly three entries in all with the belief; fewer only when the export is genuinely thin — none repeating another or restating a top motivator or a signature pattern.

topMotivators.description: Exactly three of Schwartz's ten basic values — the three that show most in what they actually do, strongest first. Read behaviour, not aspiration: what they spend time, effort and attention on.

score.description: 0-100: how strongly this value shows up in what they actually do, relative to their other nine values.

line.description: One sentence of evidence for the score. For a low score, what shows it is low, or "little in the data either way". Under 160 characters.

reading.description: Two or three sentences on the shape: what they are moving towards, and the tension between their top values if there is one.

detail.description: Two or three sentences, concrete and specific to this person.
Two or three sentences, concrete and specific to this person.

language.description: One of: "Words of affirmation", "Acts of service", "Quality time", "Receiving gifts", "Physical touch".

why.description: One or two sentences of evidence from their actual data. Say plainly when the evidence is thin.

inPractice.description: One concrete sentence: what this looks like for this person specifically, not the textbook description.

receiving.description: One to three languages they most likely want to be loved in, strongest first.

language.description: One of: "Words of affirmation", "Acts of service", "Quality time", "Receiving gifts", "Physical touch".

why.description: One or two sentences of evidence from their actual data. Say plainly when the evidence is thin.

inPractice.description: One concrete sentence: what this looks like for this person specifically, not the textbook description.

giving.description: One to three languages they most likely reach for when showing love, strongest first. These are often not the same as the ones above.

caveat.description: One sentence noting that love languages are a popular framework rather than a validated one, and that some of these — physical touch especially — barely show up in an Instagram export at all.

detail.description: Two or three sentences, concrete and specific to this person.

strengths.description: One or two work strengths other than `careerAssessment.edge` — never the edge said again in other words.

detail.description: Two or three sentences, concrete and specific to this person.

weaknesses.description: At most one: a cost at work that `careerAssessment.holdingBack` does not already name. Empty is fine.

character.description: The one character from this catalogue this person is most like in temperament — how they behave, what drives them, how they treat people; never how anyone looks.

franchise.description: The franchise the catalogue gives this character: Disney, Arthur Conan Doyle, Pixar, L. Frank Baum, Homer, Marvel, DC, Pokémon, Nintendo, DreamWorks, Harry Potter, Sailor Moon, Sanrio.

icon.description: Always an empty string: the app draws this character's emblem.

why.description: One or two sentences, under 50 words: the trait they share with this character, tied to one specific thing in their data. Name the shared trait, not the plot of the film.

summary.description: About 120 words — never more than 140 — in one or two short paragraphs, written to them as "you".

cardHighlights.description: Exactly two sentences for the shareable card, written to them as "you", condensed from the character line (`essence.why`) and the executive summary (`summary`) written just above: why they are like this character, and the person behind it at their best.

lifeTrajectory.description: Where this person appears to be in their life and which way it has been moving, read across the whole span of the export rather than from the last few months.

outlook.description: Whether they write as though things tend to work out or tend not to, and how strongly, from their own words.

socialConnection.description: The shape of their contact with other people — how many distinct people rather than how many messages, whether it reaches beyond an established circle, whether it runs both ways.

cognitiveLoad.description: How much they appear to be carrying at once, from the shape of their activity rather than any claim about their mind: how many separate threads, projects and commitments show up in what they write, how much they switch between them, whether announced plans accumulate faster than they close out.

meaning.description: What appears to give their activity a point: what they return to over years, what they show up for without being asked, whether their stated commitments and their actual behaviour agree.

rhythmAndActivity.description: Two related things read together: when they are active across the day and week, and how much physical activity shows up in what they post.

overall.description: Two or three sentences drawing the six together — where the pattern looks steady, where it looks strained, and which one or two are worth their attention first. Prose only.

suggestions.description: One or two concrete things to try this week, each tied to a dimension above and to its evidence — they go on the plan, which holds about five actions in all. Practical, never treatment, therapy or a care plan.

style.description: Name the style using one of three: secure, anxious or avoidant. Readers know these names, look them up, and compare notes with a partner, and a made-up phrase in their place leaves them with nothing to search for.

styleTone.description: One warm, plain sentence saying what this style is good at — every leaning comes with real strengths, and the reader should meet theirs before they meet the caveats.

why.description: Three or four sentences showing your working: which behavioural traces pointed here, which style you considered and rejected, and what would have changed your mind.

conflict.description: How they handle disagreement with people close to them, in two or three sentences written to them as "you": whether they raise it, smooth it over, go quiet or come in hot, in what form, and what that does to the other person — from how they respond when a thread or a comment turns tense and how they handle the gap after one.

derivedFrom.description: Two to four specific signals from the data this reading rests on, each a short phrase. Name the actual numbers or patterns.

caveat.description: State plainly that attachment style cannot be read reliably from this data.

needs.description: Three to five concrete things this person actually needs in a partner to be well in the relationship — not a list of pleasant adjectives, but requirements that follow from the attachment style above, their love languages, their rhythm and their relationship strengths and weaknesses.

carefulOf.description: Two to four honest warnings about partner types, dynamics or their own patterns worth being careful of — the kind of partner or relationship shape that would predictably go wrong for this specific person, given their attachment style, their relationship weaknesses and how they actually behave when close to someone.

summary.description: Two or three sentences drawing the needs and the cautions together into one honest, specific verdict on what kind of partner truly suits this person — direct enough to be useful on its own if a reader skips straight to it, and not a restatement of the two lists above.

headline.description: A few words naming the edge itself, e.g. "You finish what other people announce".

detail.description: Three or four sentences on what genuinely differentiates them — the thing they do reliably that most people do not, stated as an advantage they can actually use.

evidence.description: Two to four specific things from the digest that make this an edge rather than a flattering guess. Quote the real counts, rhythms or phrases.

underused.description: Something they already have and are visibly not using — a skill the data shows, a network they do not draw on, work they do that nobody sees. The gap between what they can do and what they are getting credit for.

holdingBack.description: The pattern most likely to cost them professionally, drawn from behaviour rather than from a personality label. Be direct: this is the part a coach earns their fee on. Attack the pattern, never the person.

suits.description: Three kinds of work that would suit them best, strongest first, each written as the kind of work, a colon, then one sentence on why, from something specific in their data (e.g. "Research in a small product team: …").

draining.description: Two or three kinds of work that would drain them, each written as the kind of work, a colon, then one sentence on what it would cost them, from their data.

horizon.description: When this should happen. One of: "this week", "this quarter", "this year".

title.description: A few words, phrased as something to do.

detail.description: Two or three sentences: what doing it actually looks like, concretely enough to start. Name the first move, not the ambition.

actions.description: One or two, on different horizons — the plan holds about five actions in all, and covers this week, this quarter and this year, at least one each.

title.description: A few words: the strength to lean into.

detail.description: Two sentences: what it is, and how to use it more deliberately.

pattern.description: The id of the signature pattern this comes from, or "none" if it does not come from one. One of: "p1", "p2", "p3", "none".

raisedBy.description: The sections whose findings raised this, so the reader can see why it is here.

title.description: A few words: the area worth working on.

detail.description: Two or three sentences: what the pattern costs them, from the evidence, without moralising — and the strength it comes from, tipped too far under pressure or when tired.

pattern.description: The id of the signature pattern this comes from, or "none" if it does not come from one. One of: "p1", "p2", "p3", "none".

raisedBy.description: The sections whose findings raised this.

earlySigns.description: Two observable behaviours that show this starting — things they, or someone close to them, could notice early. Behaviours, not feelings.

counterMove.description: One concrete move for the moment they notice it. One sentence.

step.description: One concrete first move, startable as written. One sentence.

actions.description: One or two actions, on different horizons — the whole plan holds about five, and between them they cover this week, this quarter and this year: at least one each.

reflect.description: One open question worth sitting with, specific to them. Not rhetorical.

headline.description: One short phrase capturing who they are at their best, drawn from the character line and the executive summary. It heads the card they share, so positive, with no negative connotation and nothing about romance or dating.

relationshipStrengths.description: Up to 2 short phrases on what they bring to friends and the people close to them, each under 34 characters. Nothing about romance or dating.

relationshipWeaknesses.description: Up to 2 short phrases on where it gets hard with friends and the people close to them, each under 34 characters. Real weaknesses, not humblebrags. Nothing about romance or dating.

careerStrengths.description: Up to 2 short phrases, each under 34 characters.

careerWeaknesses.description: Up to 2 short phrases on what holds them back at work, each under 34 characters. Real costs, not humblebrags — the same costs the full report names under what holds you back.

conflictStyle.description: How they handle disagreement, as a leaning plus "(tentative)": whether they raise it, smooth it over, go quiet or come in hot, and in what form — "Raises it calmly, in writing (tentative)", "Goes quiet, then circles back (tentative)".

rhythm.description: Their daily and social rhythm in a few words. Under 48 characters.

energy.description: How outward-facing they are and how they keep in touch: broadcaster, participant or lurker; a wide circle or a few close ties; and their contact style — who starts the conversations, how quickly and how long they reply.

workStyle.description: How they actually work — standards, follow-through, pace. Under 75 characters.

harsh.description: A send-up: two or three short paragraphs, deliberately blunt and pointed, the version a sharp friend gives when it is their turn to be teased in front of everyone. Name the contradictions and habits head-on, with the real specifics: plans announced and dropped, things saved and never done, the gap between the image they post and what the record shows. Do not soften it or balance it with compliments; the next field is where the kindness goes. Funny and true, never cruel about what they cannot change: never health, appearance, identity or anyone else. If they seem to be going through a hard time, tease only small, harmless habits.

advice.description: One or two short paragraphs of frank, kind advice that follows from the observations above: concrete, practical, and in plain words.

reading.description: Two or three sentences on what the data actually shows for this dimension, written to them as "you". the specification lists what to read for each of the six.

evidence.description: Two to four specific things from the digest behind this — a rhythm, a count, a gap, a caption. Quote the real number or phrase rather than gesturing at it.

detail.description: Two or three sentences, concrete and specific to this person.
Two or three sentences, specific to them rather than to anyone in their position.

deepSpec:
## Deep Psyche
This read is a Deep Psyche, which the user chose knowing it takes about 20 to 30 minutes. It is the same document to the same standards, from a sample about four times the reading plan's:
- **About 800,000 characters of their own words at most:** posts and stories up to about 340,000 (comments up to about 40,000 of it); messages, when they agreed, up to about 440,000, across the 20 conversations they write in most, at most about 30,000 from any one; likes, saves, follows and searches up to about 30,000.
- **A year at a time.** Read one year, oldest first, and keep short notes on it before the next: the dated moments that stand out, with counts; what keeps recurring; what started, stopped or changed since the year before. Then write the read from the notes, going back to the items themselves only for the evidence it cites.
- **How they changed is part of the read:** trajectories, patterns and the confidence rationale use the years ("ran most weeks 2019 to 2021, nothing since"), and the rationale says it was a Deep Psyche and what was read, in counts, year by year.

sync.spec:
# A PsycheAI Sync: what it contains and the standards it meets

A Sync is how two people get on: friends, family, anyone; never romance or dating. Both people agreed to it. It is written from each person's card-level profile (no report, no posts) and the derived facts, which are computed and settled. Person A is the user; person B is the other person. Each is called by the first name their profile gives.

## What it contains: the same as a Sync on psycheai.io
One object matching the schema, in this order, shown to both people as one image (so each part is short enough to read there):
1. **summary:** one warm line, under 25 words.
2. **align:** two or three points: a title of a few words, two short sentences naming both people, and the evidence behind it.
3. **differ:** two or three points, the same way, each with how the difference can work for them.
4. **howToPartner:** three things for person A (forA) and three for person B (forB), each addressed to them as "you", one sentence of under about 120 characters; and two things they could do together.
5. **caveats:** one or two sentences on what this cannot see.

## Standards
- Positive and encouraging throughout. Differences are differences with a way to make them work, never a fault in either person. No blame or labels, and no prediction that the connection will struggle.
- The words tension, conflict, clash, friction, struggle, problem and incompatible are not used; "difference", "disagreement" or "a different pace" instead.
- No score or percentage. The connection is never called a friendship or any other named relationship: "you two", "your connection".
- Types are weighed in a sentence or two at most: E/I and S/N matter most, T/F less, J/P least; a score near 50 is a lean.
- Only shared interests the derived facts list. Each point rests on something in the profiles, named in its evidence.
- Profiles are inferences from social media; if either confidence is low, it is a conversation starter rather than a finding.
sync.brief:
These two may be friends, family or anyone else close, and you are not told which. How they sync, vibe and relate turns on shared interests and activities, compatible energy, a similar appetite for contact, how each shows care, and how easily things flow between them. Whether they would actually enjoy time together matters more than any label. Nothing here is about romance or dating, and nothing should read that way.

What matters most, in this order:
  - Shared interests
  - Energy match
  - Appetite for contact
  - How easily things flow
  - Outlook and values

The fields that decide those most: interests, energy (how they keep in touch), extraversion, conflictStyle, agreeableness, values, loveReceiving and loveGiving (how each shows care).

mode.description: Echo back the basis you were asked to assess.

summary.description: One line, under 25 words: the truest warm thing about these two as connections, the line they would happily quote. No score, no rating, no "but".

detail.description: Two sentences, concrete and naming both people.

evidence.description: One or two short items naming what in the profiles put this here — a trait score, a value, how each handles a disagreement, a rhythm. Quote the actual phrase or number rather than gesturing at it. Prefer one item per person. Never reuse an item already given as evidence for a dimension or another point.

align.description: Where you align: two or three things the two of them have in common or that suit each other, sharpest first. Title a few words ("Same love of a plan"), detail one or two sentences naming both people.

detail.description: Two sentences, concrete and naming both people.

evidence.description: One or two short items naming what in the profiles put this here — a trait score, a value, how each handles a disagreement, a rhythm. Quote the actual phrase or number rather than gesturing at it. Prefer one item per person. Never reuse an item already given as evidence for a dimension or another point.

differ.description: Where you differ: two or three real differences, each titled neutrally ("Different paces") and, in the detail, how the difference can work for them (see # Tone).

forA.description: Three concrete things the FIRST person can do to relate better to the other, addressed to them as "you".

forB.description: Three concrete things the SECOND person can do to relate better to the other, addressed to them as "you".

together.description: Two things they could agree on or do together.

caveats.description: One or two sentences on what this read cannot see.
